text_blocks.snippet: High blood pressure (hypertension) is often called the "silent killer" because it typically has no signs or symptoms. Most people with high blood pressure feel completely fine and can live with it for years without knowing.
snippet_highlighted_words: it typically has no signs or symptoms

text_blocks.snippet: When Symptoms Do Appear (Dangerously High Blood Pressure / Hypertensive Crisis)
Symptoms generally do not show up until blood pressure reaches dangerously high levels—typically a reading of 180/120 mm Hg or higher.
If your blood pressure is extremely high, you may experience:

list.snippet: Blurry vision or other sudden changes in eyesight

text_blocks.snippet: What to Do in a Hypertensive Emergency
According to the American Heart Association and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention:

snippet_links.text: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

list.snippet: Wait at least 1 minute and take your blood pressure again if your reading is above 180/120 mm Hg.

If the second reading is just as high and you have any warning signs—such as chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, change in vision, or difficulty speaking—call 911 immediately.
If your reading is above 180/120 mm Hg but you do not have any of these symptoms, contact your healthcare provider right away for guidance.

text_blocks.snippet: Because you cannot rely on how you feel, regular screening is essential. Adults should have their blood pressure checked at least once a year during regular medical visits, or more frequently if recommended by a doctor. You can review detailed blood pressure categories and guidance on the Mayo Clinic High Blood Pressure Overview.

list.snippet: What your most recent blood pressure reading was (if you know it)
Whether you are experiencing any specific symptoms right now
If you have a history of high blood pressure or related conditions
